# Week 4, Day 4.1 — TypeScript for data-driven tests

Seven small things. Today one test body runs against many rows, read from a file — and by the end of
the day, from three different kinds of file.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `for...of` (and its two cousins) | walk the rows |
| 2 | `node:fs` `readFileSync` | the data lives outside the test |
| 3 | `JSON.parse` | text on disk becomes objects |
| 4 | `if` / `else if` / `else` | different rows expect different outcomes |
| 5 | `import * as X from "pkg"` | Playwright can't read Excel; a library can |
| 6 | Bracket access `obj[key]` | `workbook.Sheets[name]` — the key is a variable |
| 7 | `path.join` and `__dirname` | find the file regardless of where you ran from |

Already covered — links only: arrays and spread in [week3/day5_1](/learn/w3/d5/p1); objects in
[week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1); `===` in [week3/day4_1](/learn/w3/d4/p1); imports in
[week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1).

## 1. Three ways to loop, and which to use

| Form | Gives you | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++)` | the **index** | you need the position |
| `for (const k in obj)` | the **keys** of an object | walking an object's properties |
| `for (const item of array)` | each **value** | **almost always, for arrays** |

`for...in` on an array gives `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"` — *strings*, not the items. That surprise is why
`for...of` exists and why it's the default choice.

**Expected:** four blocks. In the `for...in` block the keys print as `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"` — quoted,
because they're strings.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

**Expected:** `string`, the file's opening, `raw.users is: undefined`, then `object | users: 3` and
three aligned lines.

That `undefined` is the point. It looks like data and it's a string — so the mistake fails quietly two
steps later rather than at the point you made it.

**Read, then parse.** Each fails differently: a bad path throws `ENOENT`, malformed JSON throws
`Unexpected token`. Knowing which tells you whether to fix the path or the file.

> `REPO_ROOT` comes from the shared helper so the path works regardless of where Jupyter started. A
> lesson's working directory is not something to rely on.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 4. `if` / `else if` / `else`

Not every row expects the same outcome. Some credentials should work; some should be refused.

**Expected:** four lines, the last flagged as unknown.

**`else if` versus `else`:** with two outcomes, `else` is enough. Once there are three you need
`else if` — and a final `else` that **fails loudly**.

Without that last branch a typo like `"dashbaord"` matches nothing, no assertion runs, and the test
**passes**. A green test that checked nothing is worse than a red one.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 5, 6 & 7. Third-party modules, bracket access, and paths

Your own files are imported by path; an npm package is imported **by name**. `import * as X` is for
modules exporting many functions and no single default — which is how the Excel library is shaped.

`obj[variable]` looks the key up at runtime, which is what you need when a sheet name comes from the
file itself. And `path.join(__dirname, …)` resolves relative to the **file**, not to wherever you ran
the command.

**Expected:** two `function` lines, `LoginCases -> {"rows":6}`, the sheet list, a joined path (with
`\` on Windows) and the hand-built one showing a doubled separator.

`workbook.Sheets.first` would look for a sheet literally named `"first"` and find nothing — giving
`undefined` rather than an error.

`__dirname` isn't available in lesson cells (they use `REPO_ROOT`), but it's the right tool in a real
spec, and it's what today's specs use.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `for...of` | Default for arrays. `for...in` gives string keys. |
| `readFileSync` | Returns **text**. Pass `"utf-8"`. |
| `JSON.parse` | Read and parse fail differently. |
| final `else` | Must **throw** — a data typo can't be allowed to pass. |
| `import * as X` | Needs `npm install` first. |
| `obj[key]` | When the key is a variable. |
| `path.join(__dirname, …)` | Relative to the file, not the shell. |

**Next:** [Day 4.2 — One test, many rows](/learn/w4/d4/p2)

# Week 4, Day 4.2 — One test, many rows

Your customer hands you twenty username/password pairs and asks whether they all work. By the end of
this lesson you answer that without writing twenty tests — and handle rows that are *supposed* to
fail.

> **Try it here.** Write code in the editor on the right and press Run. Your code drives a real browser, and the results appear beside it.

## What parameterization is, and when it isn't

Replacing hardcoded values with values from an external source. Also called **data-driven testing**.

The rule worth stating up front: **it's for multiple sets of data.** One fixed username belongs in a
helper function; parameterization would add indirection and nothing else.

Two genuinely different situations hide under the same name:

| | What varies | What you're testing |
|---|---|---|
| **Data testing** | the data | *the data* — do these 20 accounts work? |
| **Test-case-driven** | the data **and the expected result** | *the application* — does login behave correctly? |

Both appear below. The second needs one extra idea.

## Why the data leaves the test

| Hardcoded in the test | In a data file |
|---|---|
| adding a case means editing code | edit data, no code review |
| credentials sit in source | one file to keep out of git |
| 20 near-identical test bodies | one body |
| a non-developer can't contribute | they can edit it |
## Example 1 — read the file, drive the app

**Expected:**

```
records: 3
U01 Leela      -> dashboard, name shown: true
U02 Katy       -> dashboard, name shown: true
U03 Jyosthna   -> dashboard, name shown: true
```

**The log-out is not decoration.** Without it the second iteration begins on the dashboard, the email
field isn't there, and you get a confusing timeout on row 2 of a loop that worked on row 1.

Any loop driving an app needs to think about **returning to the starting state** — the most common
reason a data-driven loop passes once then fails.

**Challenge:** comment out the two log-out lines and watch which row fails, and how.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## In a spec: the loop goes *outside* `test()`

The cell above is **one** long sequence. If Katy's credentials break, the loop throws and Jyosthna is
never tried — and the report says "1 test failed", not "row 2 of 3 failed".

```ts
for (const user of testData.users) {
  test(`${user.id} — ${user.name} signs in`, async ({ page }) => { … });
}
```

| | Loop inside one test | Loop generating tests |
|---|---|---|
| Rows reported | 1 result | one per row |
| Row 2 fails | rows 3+ never run | rows 3+ still run |
| Retries | the whole loop | just the failing row |
| Runs in parallel | no | yes |

The loop runs while Playwright is **collecting** tests, before any execute. That's why it produces
three tests rather than one test that loops three times.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week4/generated/day4-data-driven.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `3 passed`, named `U01 — Leela signs in` and so on.

The spec uses `import testData from "./day4-users.json"` rather than `readFileSync` — type-checked,
with no path to get wrong. Keep `readFileSync` for formats TypeScript can't import.

And the assertion is `expect(page.getByText(user.name))` — compared against **the data**, never
against `"Leela"` typed a second time. Type it twice and a typo makes the test pass for the wrong
reason.

## When each row expects something different

Example 1 assumed every row succeeds. Real test cases don't. So the **expected result** joins the
data:

```json
{ "id": "TC02", "email": "leela@gmail.com", "password": "WrongPass1", "expected": "blocked" }
```

### What this app actually does — measured, not assumed

All six rows were probed against the live site:

| Row | Login button | Result |
|---|---|---|
| valid credentials | enabled | reaches `/dashboard`, name visible |
| correct email, wrong password | enabled | stays on login, **no message at all** |
| unknown email | enabled | stays on login, no message |
| blank email / password / both | **disabled** | cannot be clicked |

**Three kinds of outcome, not two.** The blank cases never reach the server — the button is disabled by
client-side validation, so there is no response to assert on. That only shows up if you check.

> Which connects to something worth knowing: login pages deliberately give vague feedback. "Wrong
> password" would confirm the *email* was right — useful to an attacker enumerating accounts. Generic
> or absent messaging on a login form is usually a security decision, not sloppiness.

**Expected:** three plan lines, then `TC99 -> threw: Unknown expected value: dashbaord`.

That last line is the most important thing in this lesson. **A misspelled expected value must fail
the test.** Leave the final `else` out and `"dashbaord"` matches nothing, no assertion runs, and the
test passes — a green result that verified nothing.

Note the `disabled` branch returns early: there's nothing to click, so there's no response to check.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week4/generated/day4-login-cases.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `6 passed`, one per row, each named with its id and description.

Read the test names in the output: `TC04 — blank email disables the button` tells you what failed and
why without opening the file — which is what the `id` and `description` fields are for.

## Best practices

- **Only for multiple rows.** One fixed value belongs in a helper.
- **Assert against the data**, never a repeated literal.
- **Return to the starting state** at the end of each row.
- **Loop outside `test()`** so each row is its own reported test.
- **Every row carries an expected result**, and the final `else` throws.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Row 1 passes, row 2 times out | didn't return to the start state | log out / navigate back |
| `raw.users is undefined` | forgot `JSON.parse` | parse the text first |
| `ENOENT` | wrong path | use `REPO_ROOT`, or `import` the JSON |
| `Unexpected token` in JSON | trailing comma or single quotes | double quotes, no trailing commas |
| One test result for twenty rows | loop is inside `test()` | move it outside |
| A data typo produces a green run | no final `else` | make it throw |

**Next:** [Day 4.3](/learn/w4/d4/p3) — when the data lives in a spreadsheet.

parts.title: When the data lives somewhere else

blocks.text:
# Week 4, Day 4.3 — When the data lives somewhere else

Same loop, same assertions as [Day 4.2](/learn/w4/d4/p2). What changes is **where the rows come from** —
because on a real project you rarely get to choose JSON.

## Playwright reads JSON. Everything else converts to it.

That's the whole model, and saying it plainly makes every format the same problem:

| Format | Needs | Becomes |
|---|---|---|
| JSON | nothing — native | objects |
| CSV | `npm install csv` | objects |
| Excel | `npm install xlsx` | objects |

Read the file, convert to objects, loop. Only the middle step changes.

## Excel: workbook → sheet → cell

Three words the library uses literally: a **workbook** is the file, a **sheet** is one tab, a **cell**
is one box.

**Expected:**

```
sheets in this workbook: [ "LoginCases" ]
rows: 6
first row: {"id":"TC01",...}
TC04 email: " "
```

Two things worth stopping on.

**That last line is a real gotcha.** TC04 is the "blank email" case — and it comes back as a **space**,
not an empty string. A *truly* empty cell is dropped by `sheet_to_json` entirely: the key disappears
and `row.email` becomes `undefined`. The session hit this live, and the fix was to type a space into
the blank cells. So your test must treat whitespace-only as blank — `.trim()` before deciding.

**We used `XLSX.read(bytes)`, not `XLSX.readFile(path)`.** `readFile` needs the library's filesystem
wiring, which isn't present in every module system — it throws `XLSX.readFile is not a function`.
Reading the bytes yourself works everywhere, and matches the CSV shape below.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## CSV: comma separated values

Lighter than Excel, diffable in git, openable anywhere. Playwright's own documentation shows this
pattern — a good sign it's the sane default.

**Expected:** `6`, the first row, and `same as the Excel rows: true`.

Both options earn their place:

- `columns: true` — without it you get **arrays**, so `row[2]` replaces `row.email`. Set it `false` and
  row 1 becomes data: your header row gets tested as a login attempt.
- `skip_empty_lines: true` — a trailing newline otherwise becomes an empty row, and an empty row
  becomes a test case with no data.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Before you reach for Excel: a real caveat

`npm install xlsx` pulls a package with **two high-severity advisories and no fix available**:

| Advisory | Affects |
|---|---|
| Prototype Pollution — GHSA-4r6h-8v6p-xvw6 | every version on npm |
| ReDoS — GHSA-5pgg-2g8v-p4x9 | every version on npm |

`npm audit` reports `fixAvailable: false`, and the version npm serves is **0.18.5** — from 2022.
SheetJS moved its maintained builds to its own CDN; the npm copy was left behind.

That is why the session's students kept hitting blocked installs and self-signed-certificate errors:
their corporate networks were refusing the package deliberately. The instructor's instinct that these
are *"very unsecure library"* was right.

| Option | When |
|---|---|
| **Use CSV instead** | almost always — same data, no advisory, diffable |
| Install SheetJS from its own CDN | you genuinely need `.xlsx` features |
| Convert `.xlsx` → `.csv` once, commit the CSV | analysts own the spreadsheet, tests read the CSV |

Know the Excel technique — you'll inherit suites that use it. Reach for CSV by default.

## Pick a format by who edits the file

| Format | Edited by | Diffs in git | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **JSON** | developers | yes, cleanly | native |
| **CSV** | anyone with a text editor or Excel | yes, cleanly | one small library |
| **Excel** | analysts, business, QA leads | **no** — binary blob | a library with open advisories |

That "diffs in git" column decides more arguments than performance ever will. A CSV change shows up in
review as *"TC07 expected message changed"*. An `.xlsx` change shows up as *"binary file modified"* —
unreviewable, and unmergeable if two people edit it.

**The pattern that works when analysts own the data:** they keep the spreadsheet wherever they like,
and a one-line export produces the CSV the repo reads. Humans get Excel, git gets text.
## The same six cases, from both files

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week4/generated/day4-excel-csv.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `14 passed` — 6 cases × 2 sources, plus 2 tests proving the sources agree.

The cell writes the **CSV** but not the `.xlsx`: a spreadsheet is binary and can't be embedded in a
text cell. It's already in `week4/generated/`, and Day 4.4 has you build one.

The spec's most important line isn't about file formats at all:

```ts
const email = testCase.email.trim();
```

That's the blank-cell gotcha, handled. Without it TC04 types a space, the Login button enables, and
the test fails asserting `toBeDisabled()` — for a reason with nothing to do with the application.

## Test data is not always safe to commit

A file of usernames and passwords is a file of credentials, whatever you call it.

| Data | Commit it? |
|---|---|
| Demo credentials for a public sandbox | yes — this repo does, deliberately |
| Real usernames for a staging environment | **no** — env vars or a secret store |
| Customer names, emails, card numbers | **never** |
| Generated fixtures | yes, and regenerate rather than hand-edit |

Git keeps history: committing a credential and deleting it next commit does not remove it.

## What a reviewer checks

- **Is Excel earning its cost?** If nobody outside the team edits it, CSV is strictly better.
- **Is the data reviewable?** A binary diff in a pull request is a red flag.
- **Any real credentials** in a committed data file?
- **`.trim()` on spreadsheet values**, and `columns: true` on CSV.
- **Dependencies audited** — `fixAvailable: false` deserves a conversation, not a shrug.

**Next:** [Day 4.4](/learn/w4/d4/p4) — your turn.

# Week 4, Day 4.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

Files to copy the shape from: `week4/generated/day4-users.json`, `day4-login-cases.json`,
`day4-excel-csv.csv` and `.xlsx`.

Verified login behaviour: valid → `/dashboard` with the name visible; wrong credentials → stays on
login with **no message**; any blank field → Login button **disabled**.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 4.1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) or [Day 4.2](/learn/w4/d4/p2).

## When you're done

**Your equality test is the useful one.** When three sources hold the same data, the bug is almost
never parsing — it's that someone edited one file and forgot the others. A test comparing the sources
catches that in seconds.

**And the misspelling check matters most.** A data-driven suite where a typo in the data produces a
green run is the most dangerous shape in this course — it looks like coverage and isn't.

**Next:** [Day 5.1](/learn/w4/d5/p1) — testing what a page *looks* like.

problems.statement:
**Build.** A data file and a spec that generates one test per row.

1. A CSV with the three demo accounts (`id,name,email,password`)
2. Read it with `csv-parse/sync` and `columns: true`
3. Loop **outside** `test()` so each account is its own test; sign in, assert the name from the data,
   sign out

**Check yourself.** Three separately-named tests pass. Then break **one** password in the file and
confirm exactly one test fails and the other two still run. Then set `columns: false` and describe
what breaks.

> **Hint** — if breaking one row makes all three vanish from the report, your loop is inside `test()`.

**Build.** The same data in Excel, and find the empty-cell trap yourself.

1. Create an `.xlsx` with those three accounts — in Excel, or with `XLSX.utils.json_to_sheet` and
   `XLSX.writeFile` in a small script
2. Read it with `XLSX.read` + `sheet_to_json`; assert the Excel rows and CSV rows are **deeply equal**
3. Now leave one cell **genuinely empty** (delete its contents) and read again
4. Extend `day4-login-cases` with two rows you design: an email with no `@`, and a valid password
   padded with spaces. **Predict** each `expected` before running

**Check yourself.** Step 2 passes. Step 3 shows the key **missing entirely** — state what
`row.<field>` returns and what that does to a test. For step 4, note any prediction you got wrong.

> **Hint** — step 3 is the failure the session hit live. Step 4's space-padded password is a real-world
> bug source; decide whether the behaviour you find is correct.

**Build.** One loader, three formats, one test body.

Read the same six login cases from **JSON, CSV and Excel** and run the identical test body against all
three.

1. A single `loadCases(file)` that picks its parser from the file **extension**
2. One loop over the three files, generating `6 × 3 = 18` tests
3. Test names that make the source obvious
4. A test asserting all three sources parse to deeply-equal data

**Where.** A spec in `week4/generated/`, plus whatever data files you need.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **One test body.** If you wrote it three times, the exercise didn't land.
- Whitespace-only values treated as blank
- A final `else` that **throws** on an unrecognised expected value
- Every test passes **run on its own**

Then answer in a comment: *which of the three would you actually ship, and what would have to be true
for you to choose Excel?*

**Check yourself.** 19 tests pass. Then break **one** value in **one** file: exactly one test fails
*and* the equality test fails, telling you which source drifted. Then add a row with a misspelled
expected value and confirm it **fails** rather than silently passing.

> **Hint** — `path.extname()` gives you the extension. The comment question has a real answer: Excel
> wins exactly when someone outside the team owns the data.
